supremeCourt.name: Tribunal Supremo de Justicia (TSJ)
supremeCourt.fspEraChanges: Widely documented capture: the 2004 Organic Law expanded the TSJ from 20 to 32 magistrates, giving the government a majority; in Dec 2015 the outgoing pro-government Assembly appointed 13 magistrates before the opposition majority was seated. The TSJ subsequently annulled or curtailed acts of the opposition-led National Assembly (2016–2017).
supremeCourt.stillServing: The court has remained PSUV-aligned ever since the 2004 expansion and 2015 packing; a 2022 reform cut it to 20 magistrates, re-appointed by the chavista-controlled National Assembly. No independent/opposition-appointed bloc remains.

courtHistory.event: The high court evolved from the Corte Federal y de Casación (Gómez era) to the Corte Suprema de Justicia under the 1961 Constitution.
The Bolivarian Constitution (Chávez) replaced the Corte Suprema with the Tribunal Supremo de Justicia (TSJ).
The Organic Law of the TSJ expanded the court from 20 to 32 magistrates, giving the government a majority — the decisive court-packing.
In December the outgoing pro-government National Assembly appointed 13 magistrates before the newly-elected opposition majority was seated.
The TSJ annulled or curtailed acts of the opposition-led National Assembly, including the March 2017 rulings stripping it of its powers (later partly walked back).
A reform of the Organic Law reduced the TSJ from 32 to 20 magistrates, who were re-appointed by the chavista-controlled Assembly — keeping the court government-aligned.

supremeCourt.justicesNote: The TSJ has had 20–32 magistrates; individual members are not itemized here. The court has been PSUV/government-aligned since the 2004 packing, with no opposition-appointed bloc.

fspParties.note: PSUV (and its predecessor MVR) is the FSP governing party. Regalado's 2007 roster also lists the Partido Comunista de Venezuela (PCV), Movimiento Electoral del Pueblo and Liga Socialista; the PCV broke with the PSUV around 2020.

legislativeControl.seats: Chavismo (MVR) emerged only in 1998; the pre-1999 bicameral Congreso was dominated by AD and COPEI.
Chavista majority in the unicameral Asamblea Nacional from 2000; near-total after the opposition boycotted 2005; a majority (not two-thirds) after 2010.
The opposition (MUD) won a two-thirds Assembly majority in Dec 2015; the PSUV became the legislative minority.
legislativeControl.notes: PSUV kept the presidency and, from 2017, governed through the all-Chavista Constituent Assembly (ANC); the Supreme Tribunal stripped the opposition-led Assembly of its powers. The opposition and many governments rejected the ANC.

legislativeControl.seats: The 2020 election (Assembly expanded to 277 seats) gave the PSUV-led Gran Polo Patriótico a supermajority.
legislativeControl.notes: The opposition boycotted the 2020 election and many governments did not recognise the result; it is disputed.
